claim: Methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR) is found in strictly anaerobic methanogenic and methanotrophic archaea.
source: Methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR), found in strictly anaerobic methanogenic and methanotrophic archaea, catalyzes the reversible production and consumption of the potent greenhouse gas methane.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: MCR catalyzes the reversible production and consumption of methane.
source: Methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR), found in strictly anaerobic methanogenic and methanotrophic archaea, catalyzes the reversible production and consumption of the potent greenhouse gas methane.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the chemical equation and citations in the introduction.

claim: The α subunit of MCR (McrA) contains several unusual post-translational modifications, including a rare thioamidation of glycine.
source: The α subunit of MCR (McrA) contains several unusual post-translational modifications, including a rare thioamidation of glycine.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The archaeal tfuA and ycaO genes are responsible for post-translational installation of thioglycine into McrA.
source: Based on the presumed function of homologous genes involved in the biosynthesis of thioviridamide, a thioamide-containing natural product, we hypothesized that the archaeal tfuA and ycaO genes would be responsible for post-translational installation of thioglycine into McrA.
evidence: This hypothesis is tested and confirmed by mass spectrometry data showing loss of thioglycine in deletion mutants.

claim: McrA from Methanosarcina acetivorans lacking tfuA and/or ycaO contains glycine rather than thioglycine at position 465.
source: Mass spectrometric characterization of McrA from the methanogenic archaeon Methanosarcina acetivorans lacking tfuA and/or ycaO revealed the presence of glycine, rather than thioglycine, supporting this hypothesis.
evidence: This is directly supported by MALDI-TOF-MS and HR-ESI-MS/MS data showing a 16 Da mass difference consistent with oxygen replacing sulfur.

claim: The ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant has a severe growth rate defect on substrates with low free energy yields.
source: Phenotypic characterization of the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant revealed a severe growth rate defect on substrates with low free energy yields and at elevated temperatures (39°C - 45°C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate measurements on different substrates shown in Table 1.

claim: The ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant has a severe growth rate defect at elevated temperatures (39°C - 45°C).
source: Phenotypic characterization of the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant revealed a severe growth rate defect on substrates with low free energy yields and at elevated temperatures (39°C - 45°C).
evidence: This is supported by growth rate data at different temperatures shown in Figure 5.

claim: Thioglycine plays a role in stabilizing the protein secondary structure near the active site of MCR.
source: Our analyses support a role for thioglycine in stabilizing the protein secondary structure near the active site.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis, growth phenotypes, and melting temperature data.

claim: MCR catalyzes the conversion of methyl-coenzyme M (CoM) and coenzyme B (CoB) to methane and a CoB-CoM heterodisulfide.
source: Methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR) is a unique enzyme found exclusively in anaerobic archaea, where it catalyzes the reversible conversion of methyl-coenzyme M (CoM, 2-methylmercaptoethanesulfonate) and coenzyme B (CoB, 7-thioheptanoylthreoninephosphate) to methane and a CoB-CoM heterodisulfide (Ermler et al., 1997; Scheller et al., 2010):
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations and a chemical equation.

claim: The MCR reaction has been proposed to proceed via a methyl radical intermediate.
source: This reaction, which has been proposed to proceed via an unprecedented methyl radical intermediate (Wongnate et al., 2016), plays a critical role in the global carbon cycle (Thauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wongnate et al., 2016.

claim: MCR plays a critical role in the global carbon cycle.
source: This reaction, which has been proposed to proceed via an unprecedented methyl radical intermediate (Wongnate et al., 2016), plays a critical role in the global carbon cycle (Thauer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Thauer et al., 2008.

claim: MCR displays an α2β2γ2 protein domain architecture.
source: MCR displays an α2β2γ2 protein domain architecture and contains two molecules of F430, a nickel porphinoid cofactor (Ermler et al., 1997; Zheng et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: MCR contains two molecules of F430, a nickel porphinoid cofactor.
source: MCR displays an α2β2γ2 protein domain architecture and contains two molecules of F430, a nickel porphinoid cofactor (Ermler et al., 1997; Zheng et al., 2016; Moore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The reduced Ni(I) form of F430 is essential for MCR catalysis.
source: The reduced Ni(I) form of F430 is essential for catalysis (Goubeaud et al., 1997), but is highly sensitive to oxidative inactivation, a feature that renders biochemical characterization of MCR especially challenging.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goubeaud et al., 1997.

claim: The reduced Ni(I) form of F430 is highly sensitive to oxidative inactivation.
source: The reduced Ni(I) form of F430 is essential for catalysis (Goubeaud et al., 1997), but is highly sensitive to oxidative inactivation, a feature that renders biochemical characterization of MCR especially challenging.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: McrA contains methylated amino acids including 3-methylhistidine, S-methylcysteine, 5(S)-methylarginine, and 2(S)-methylglutamine.
source: Among these are a group of methylated amino acids, including 3-methylhistidine (or N1-methylhistidine), S-methylcysteine, 5(S)-methylarginine, and 2(S)-methylglutamine, which are presumed to be installed post-translationally by S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferases (Selmer et al., 2000; Kahnt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The methylated amino acids in McrA are presumed to be installed post-translationally by S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferases.
source: Among these are a group of methylated amino acids, including 3-methylhistidine (or N1-methylhistidine), S-methylcysteine, 5(S)-methylarginine, and 2(S)-methylglutamine, which are presumed to be installed post-translationally by S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferases (Selmer et al., 2000; Kahnt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: 3-methylhistidine is found in all MCRs examined to date.
source: 3-methylhistidine is found in all MCRs examined to date, whereas the presence of the other methylated amino acids is variable among methane-metabolizing archaea (Kahnt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kahnt et al., 2007.

claim: The presence of methylated amino acids other than 3-methylhistidine is variable among methane-metabolizing archaea.
source: 3-methylhistidine is found in all MCRs examined to date, whereas the presence of the other methylated amino acids is variable among methane-metabolizing archaea (Kahnt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kahnt et al., 2007.

claim: A didehydroaspartate modification is observed in some, but not all, methanogens.
source: A didehydroaspartate modification is also observed in some, but not all, methanogens (Wagner et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wagner et al., 2016.

claim: A thioglycine modification is present in all methanogens that have been analyzed to date.
source: Lastly, a highly unusual thioglycine modification, in which the peptide amide bond is converted to a thioamide, is present in all methanogens that have been analyzed to date (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Ermler et al., 1997; Kahnt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The 3-methylhistidine in McrA may serve to position the imidazole ring that coordinates CoB.
source: The 3-methylhistidine may serve to position the imidazole ring that coordinates CoB.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the introduction.

claim: Methylation of histidine alters the pKa in a manner that would promote tighter CoB-binding.
source: This methylation also alters the pKa of histidine in a manner that would promote tighter CoB-binding (Grabarse et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grabarse et al., 2000.

claim: The variable occurrence of methylated amino acids other than 3-methylhistidine suggests they are unlikely to be directly involved in catalysis.
source: The variable occurrence of the other methylated amino acids suggests that they are unlikely to be directly involved in catalysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variable presence of these modifications.

claim: Variable methylated amino acids may tune enzyme activity by altering the hydrophobicity and flexibility of the active site pocket.
source: Rather, it has been hypothesized that they tune enzyme activity by altering the hydrophobicity and flexibility of the active site pocket (Kahnt et al., 2007; Grabarse et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Thioglycine may facilitate deprotonation of CoB by reducing the pKa of the sulfhydryl group.
source: One proposal is that the thioglycine facilitates deprotonation of CoB by reducing the pKa of the sulfhydryl group (Grabarse et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Thioglycine could serve as an intermediate electron carrier for oxidation of a proposed heterodisulfide anion radical intermediate.
source: A second proposal suggests that thioglycine could serve as an intermediate electron carrier for oxidation of a proposed heterodisulfide anion radical intermediate (Horng et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Cis-trans isomerization of the thioamide during catalysis could play a role in coupling the two active sites via a two-stroke mechanism.
source: Lastly, cis-trans isomerization of the thioamide during catalysis could potentially play an important role in coupling the two active sites via a previously proposed two-stroke mechanism for the enzyme (Goenrich et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Thioamides are rare in biology.
source: Thioamides are rare in biology.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge and supported by the limited examples provided.

claim: Cycasthioamide is plant-derived.
source: While cycasthioamide is plant-derived (Pan et al., 1997), most other naturally occurring thioamides are of bacterial origin.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 1997.

claim: Most naturally occurring thioamides are of bacterial origin.
source: While cycasthioamide is plant-derived (Pan et al., 1997), most other naturally occurring thioamides are of bacterial origin.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge with examples provided.

claim: Thioviridamide is a ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified (RiPP) peptide natural product.
source: Among these are the ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified (RiPP) peptide natural products thioviridamide (Hayakawa et al., 2006) and methanobactin (Kim et al., 2004; Kenney and Rosenzweig, 2012; Kenney and Rosenzweig, 2013), as well as closthioamide, which appears to be an unusual non-ribosomal peptide (Lincke et al., 2010; Chiriac et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The thioviridamide biosynthetic gene cluster encodes TvaH, a member of the YcaO superfamily.
source: Two of the proteins encoded by this gene cluster have plausible roles in thioamide synthesis. The first, TvaH, is a member of the YcaO superfamily, while the second, TvaI, is annotated as a 'TfuA-like' protein (Izawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Izawa et al., 2013.

claim: The thioviridamide biosynthetic gene cluster encodes TvaI, annotated as a 'TfuA-like' protein.
source: Two of the proteins encoded by this gene cluster have plausible roles in thioamide synthesis. The first, TvaH, is a member of the YcaO superfamily, while the second, TvaI, is annotated as a 'TfuA-like' protein (Izawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Izawa et al., 2013.

claim: YcaO-family proteins catalyze the ATP-dependent cyclodehydration of Cys, Ser, and Thr residues to the corresponding thiazoline, oxazoline, and methyloxazoline.
source: Biochemical analyses of YcaO-family proteins indicate that they catalyze the ATP-dependent cyclodehydration of Cys, Ser, and Thr residues to the corresponding thiazoline, oxazoline, and methyloxazoline (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical studies and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: YcaO homologs are universally present in methanogen genomes.
source: Given their putative role in thioamidation reactions, it is notable that YcaO homologs were found to be universally present in an early analysis of methanogen genomes, resulting in their designation as 'methanogenesis marker protein 1' (Basu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Basu et al., 2011.

claim: Genes encoding TfuA homologs are ubiquitous in methanogens.
source: Genes encoding TfuA homologs are also ubiquitous in methanogens, usually encoded in the same locus as ycaO, similar to their arrangement in the thioviridamide biosynthetic gene cluster.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: All complete methanogen and ANME genome sequences encode a YcaO homolog.
source: Significantly, all complete methanogen and ANME genome sequences encode a YcaO homolog, with a few strains encoding two copies (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The YcaO sequences form a distinct, well-supported clade that includes homologs from ammonia-oxidizing archaea.
source: The YcaO sequences form a distinct, well-supported clade that also includes homologs from ammonia-oxidizing archaea (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The YcaO tree is congruent with the phylogeny of methanogens reconstructed using housekeeping or mcr genes.
source: Excluding the second YcaO in strains that encode two copies, the YcaO tree is congruent with the phylogeny of methanogens reconstructed using housekeeping or mcr genes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: YcaO was likely acquired early in the evolution of methanogens and maintained largely through vertical inheritance.
source: Thus, it is likely that YcaO was acquired early in the evolution of methanogens and maintained largely through vertical inheritance, as expected for a trait that coevolved with MCR (Borrel et al., 2013; Vanwonterghem et al., 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic congruence and supported by citations.

claim: TfuA homologs are encoded in the overwhelming majority of MCR-encoding taxa.
source: TfuA homologs are encoded in the overwhelming majority of MCR-encoding taxa, although a few species lack this gene.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Methanopyrus kandleri and Methanocaldococcus janaschii lack the tfuA gene but contain the thioglycine modification.
source: The latter include Methanopyrus kandleri and Methanocaldococcus janaschii, two species previously shown to contain the thioglycine modification (Kahnt et al., 2007) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kahnt et al., 2007 and shown in Figure 2.

claim: TfuA cannot be obligatorily required for thioglycine installation.
source: Thus, TfuA cannot be obligatorily required for thioglycine installation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some species lack tfuA but have thioglycine.

claim: The genomic context of tfuA and ycaO in methanogens supports a shared or related function involving sulfur incorporation and/or methanogenesis.
source: The genomic context of tfuA and ycaO in methanogens supports a shared or related function, perhaps involving sulfur incorporation and/or methanogenesis (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the gene neighborhood analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: When both tfuA and ycaO are present, they comprise a single locus where the stop codon of ycaO overlaps with the start codon of tfuA.
source: When both are present, the two genes comprise a single locus in which the stop codon of the upstream ycaO gene overlaps with the start codon of the downstream tfuA gene, suggesting that they are co-transcribed.
evidence: This is observed from genomic analysis and suggests co-transcription.

claim: Deletion of the ycaO-tfuA locus has no impact on viability of Methanosarcina acetivorans.
source: Our data demonstrate that deletion of the ycaO-tfuA locus has no impact on viability (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the Cas9-based essentiality assay shown in Figure 3.

claim: The mass spectrum from wild-type M. acetivorans showed a peak at m/z 3432 Da corresponding to the thioglycine-containing peptide.
source: The mass spectrum from the WT strain showed a peak at m/z 3432 Da (Figure 4) corresponding to the peptide (461LGFFGFDLQDQCGATNVLSYQGDEGLPDELR491) with Gly465 being thioamidated (Kahnt et al., 2007; Grabarse et al., 2000).
evidence: This is directly shown by MALDI-TOF-MS data in Figure 4.

claim: The m/z 3432 Da species is absent in the ∆ycaO-tfuA, ∆tfuA, and ∆ycaO samples.
source: Consistent with the involvement of TfuA-associated YcaO proteins in thioamide formation, we noted the absence of the m/z 3432 Da species in the mass spectrum of similarly treated ∆ycaO-tfuA, ∆tfuA, and ∆ycaO samples.
evidence: This is directly shown by MALDI-TOF-MS data in Figure 4.

claim: A predominant m/z 3416 Da species appeared in the mutant samples, which is 16 Da lighter than the wild-type peptide.
source: Instead, a predominant m/z 3416 Da species appeared, which was 16 Da lighter, consistent with replacement of sulfur by oxygen (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly shown by MALDI-TOF-MS data in Figure 4.

claim: The 16 Da mass difference is consistent with replacement of sulfur by oxygen.
source: Instead, a predominant m/z 3416 Da species appeared, which was 16 Da lighter, consistent with replacement of sulfur by oxygen (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the mass difference and confirmed by HR-ESI-MS/MS.

claim: Fragmentation between Gly465 and Phe466 was not observed in the wild-type thioamide-containing peptide during HR-ESI-MS/MS analysis.
source: During HR-ESI-MS/MS analysis of the WT, thioamide-containing peptide, we did not observe fragmentation between Gly465 and Phe466.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MS/MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fragmentation between Gly465 and Phe466 was observed in the ∆ycaO-tfuA strain peptide.
source: In contrast, fragmentation was seen at this location in the ∆ycaO-tfuA strain (b5 ion, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the MS/MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The lack of fragmentation in the wild-type peptide is due to the greater double bond character of C-N bonds in thioamides.
source: The lack of fragmentation in the WT peptide was anticipated based on the greater double bond character of C-N bonds in thioamides (Wiberg and Rablen, 1995).
evidence: This is inferred from chemical properties of thioamides and supported by a citation.

claim: Complementation of the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant with ycaO-tfuA restores the thioglycine modification.
source: To confirm that mutations in ycaO and/or tfuA were responsible for loss of the thioglycine modification, we transformed the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant with a self-replicating plasmid containing the ycaO-tfuA locus fused to the tetracycline-inducible promoter PmcrB(tetO4) (Guss et al., 2008). Upon tryptic digestion of MCR from cultures supplemented with tetracycline, a peak at m/z 3432 Da reappeared (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly shown by MALDI-TOF-MS data in Figure 4.

claim: Complementation of the ∆ycaO or ∆tfuA single mutants with the respective genes restores the thioglycine modification.
source: Similar results were obtained when complementation experiments were performed with the ycaO or tfuA genes in the corresponding single mutants (Figure 4).
evidence: This is directly shown by MALDI-TOF-MS data in Figure 4.

claim: Thioglycine formation is not a prerequisite for N-methylhistidine modification.
source: We also observed a peak at m/z 1496 in the WT and mutant samples corresponding to a N-methylhistidine-containing tryptic peptide (His271-Arg284, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A). Thus, thioglycine formation is not a prerequisite for this modification.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Gln420 remains unmodified in M. acetivorans.
source: Additionally, a peak at m/z 1561 was observed, corresponding to McrA Phe408-Arg421, shows that Gln420 remains unmodified in M. acetivorans, as previously been observed for Methanosarcina barkeri (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B) (Kahnt et al., 2007).
evidence: This is directly observed in the MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B and supported by a citation.

claim: No significant differences in growth were observed between wild-type and ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant on methanol or trimethylamine at 36°C.
source: While no significant differences were observed during growth on methanol or trimethylamine (TMA) at 36°C, the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant had substantially longer generation times and lower cell yields on both dimethylsulfide (DMS) and acetate (Table 1).
evidence: This is directly shown by growth rate measurements in Table 1.

claim: The ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant had substantially longer generation times and lower cell yields on dimethylsulfide and acetate.
source: While no significant differences were observed during growth on methanol or trimethylamine (TMA) at 36°C, the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant had substantially longer generation times and lower cell yields on both dimethylsulfide (DMS) and acetate (Table 1).
evidence: This is directly shown by growth rate measurements in Table 1.

claim: The growth phenotype on methanol medium is strongly temperature-dependent.
source: Interestingly, the growth phenotype on methanol medium was strongly temperature-dependent, with no observed differences at 29°C and 36°C, but severe defects observed for the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant at 39°C and 42°C.
evidence: This is directly shown by growth rate measurements at different temperatures in Figure 5.

claim: The ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant is incapable of growth at 45°C.
source: Furthermore, unlike WT, the mutant was incapable of growth at 45°C (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly shown by growth rate measurements in Figure 5.

claim: The melting temperature of wild-type MCR is 67.3 ± 0.3°C.
source: Using the SYPRO Orange-based Thermofluor assay (Huynh and Partch, 2015), the melting temperature of WT MCR was 67.3 ± 0.3°C (mean ± 95% confidence interval of three technical replicates) whereas the melting temperature for the MCR variant lacking thioglycine was 69.1 ± 0.2°C.
evidence: This is directly measured using the Thermofluor assay.

claim: The melting temperature of MCR from the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant is 69.1 ± 0.2°C.
source: Using the SYPRO Orange-based Thermofluor assay (Huynh and Partch, 2015), the melting temperature of WT MCR was 67.3 ± 0.3°C (mean ± 95% confidence interval of three technical replicates) whereas the melting temperature for the MCR variant lacking thioglycine was 69.1 ± 0.2°C.
evidence: This is directly measured using the Thermofluor assay.

claim: The F430 content is not significantly affected by the presence of thioglycine.
source: Additionally, quantification of the protein and F430 concentrations by Bradford assay and absorption at 280/430 nm demonstrated that the F430 content was not significantly affected by the presence of thioglycine (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly measured by UV-Vis spectroscopy shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both ycaO and tfuA genes are required for the thioamidation of McrA.
source: The loss of the thioglycine modification in the ∆ycaO, ∆tfuA, and ΔycaO-tfuA mutants shows that both of these genes are required for the thioamidation of McrA.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by mass spectrometry data from the mutants.

claim: The YcaO/TfuA proteins likely directly catalyze modification of McrA.
source: Although this could be an indirect requirement, we believe it is more likely that the YcaO/TfuA proteins directly catalyze modification of McrA.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and biochemical data, though not definitively proven.

claim: YcaO enzymes coordinate the nucleophilic attack of the Cys, Ser, and Thr side chain on the preceding amide carbonyl carbon.
source: Such cyclodehydratases coordinate the nucleophilic attack of the Cys, Ser, and Thr side chain on the preceding amide carbonyl carbon in a fashion reminiscent of intein splicing (Perler et al., 1997) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical studies and a citation.

claim: An exogenous equivalent of sulfide is required for the thioamidation reaction.
source: The only difference is that an exogenous equivalent of sulfide is required for the thioamidation reaction, rather than an adjacent beta-nucleophile-containing amino acid for azoline formation (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism shown in Figure 1.

claim: Most YcaO cyclodehydratases require a partner protein for catalytic activity.
source: Most YcaO cyclodehydratases require a partner protein for catalytic activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: TfuA may facilitate binding to the peptidic substrate.
source: Considering these traits of azoline-forming YcaOs, it is possible that thioamide-forming YcaOs require the TfuA partner to facilitate binding to the peptidic substrate.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known function of YcaO partner proteins.

claim: TfuA may recruit and deliver sulfide equivalents by a direct or indirect mechanism.
source: Alternatively, TfuA may recruit and deliver sulfide equivalents by a direct or indirect mechanism.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the genomic context and known sulfur metabolism.

claim: The ycaO-tfuA locus can be found adjacent to genes involved in sulfur and molybdoterin metabolism.
source: In this regard, it is noteworthy that the ycaO-tfuA locus can be found adjacent to genes involved in sulfur and molybdoterin metabolism (Figure 2).
evidence: This is directly shown by genomic context analysis in Figure 2.

claim: The viability of the ΔycaO-tfuA mutant precludes the hypothesis that the thioamide residue is essential for MCR activity.
source: As MCR is essential for growth and survival (Rother et al., 2005), the viability of ycaO-tfuA mutants precludes the hypothesis that the thioamide residue is essential for MCR activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the viability of the mutant and the essentiality of MCR.

claim: The most pronounced growth defects were observed with growth substrates that support the slowest wild-type growth rates.
source: Although it has not been explicitly determined, MCR is thought to catalyze the rate-limiting step of methanogenesis (Scheller et al., 2010; Wongnate et al., 2016). Therefore, the absence of thioglycine might lead to a corresponding decrease in the growth rate, with more pronounced defects on substrates that lead to the fastest growth. However, we observed the opposite: the most pronounced defects were observed with growth substrates that support the slowest WT growth rates (Table 1).
evidence: This is directly observed from the growth rate data in Table 1.

claim: Intracellular levels of methyl-CoM, CoM, and CoB could be significantly different depending on the entry point into the methanogenic pathway.
source: Significantly, these entry points are separated by an energy-dependent step that is coupled to production or consumption of the trans-membrane Na+ gradient. As a result, intracellular levels of methyl-CoM, CoM, and CoB could possibly be significantly different depending on the entry point into the methanogenic pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the metabolic pathway shown in Figure 6.

claim: The growth deficiency phenotype is unlikely to be related to changes in substrate affinity.
source: Because we observed growth defects on substrates that enter at both points (i.e. DMS and acetate), we suspect that the growth deficiency phenotype is unlikely to be related to changes in substrate affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of defects on multiple substrates.

claim: Unstable MCR protein would need to be replaced more often, creating a significant metabolic burden for the mutant.
source: A third explanation we considered was that thioglycine increases the stability of MCR. In this model, unstable MCR protein would need to be replaced more often, creating a significant metabolic burden for the mutant.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the growth phenotypes.

claim: MCR comprises approximately 10% of the total protein in methanogens.
source: Consistent with our results, this additional burden would be exacerbated on lower energy substrates like DMS and acetate, especially given that MCR comprises ~10% of the total protein (Rospert et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rospert et al., 1990.

claim: The melting temperature of MCR from the ∆ycaO-tfuA mutant is modestly higher than that purified from the wild-type.
source: However, the melting temperature of MCR from the ∆ycao-tfuA mutant was modestly higher than that purified from the WT.
evidence: This is directly measured using the Thermofluor assay.

claim: Thioamidation does not affect the global stability of MCR.
source: As the thioglycine is buried deep within the active site of MCR (Ermler et al., 1997), these data are consistent with the notion that thioamidation does not affect the global stability of the protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the melting temperature data and structural information.

claim: The thioglycine modification impacts the local stability in the vicinity of the buried active site of MCR.
source: Instead, it suggests that the thioglycine modification impacts the local stability in the vicinity of the buried active site of MCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which in turn might have a detrimental effect under catalytic turnover conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the melting temperature data, growth phenotypes, and structural analysis.

claim: Amides have lower rotational barriers than thioamides.
source: Although amides tend to be planar, their rotational barriers are lower than for the corresponding thioamide and thus they are more conformationally flexible.
evidence: This is stated as chemical knowledge.

claim: The thioamide carbonyl is not polarized like an amide carbonyl.
source: Considering the negligible electronegativity difference between sulfur and carbon, the thioamide carbonyl is not polarized like an amide carbonyl (Wiberg and Rablen, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as chemical knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The thioamide bond length is approximately 40% longer than the amide bond.
source: Further, sulfur has a larger van der Waals radius than oxygen resulting in a thioamide bond length that is ~40% longer than the amide bond (1.71 Å versus 1.23 Å) (Petersson et al., 2014), which presents additional steric hindrances to backbone flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as chemical knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The pKa of thioamides is lower than amides, making thioglycine a stronger hydrogen bond donor than glycine.
source: Finally, the pKa of thioamides is lower than amides, making thioglycine a stronger hydrogen bond donor than glycine (Lee et al., 2002), which again could reduce conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is stated as chemical knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The increased flexibility of unmodified glycine in the ΔycaO-tfuA mutant would render the contorted conformation of the peptide backbone in the Gly462-Leu469 region less stable.
source: Taken together, it is chemically reasonable to state that the increased flexibility of the unmodified glycine in the ΔycaO-tfuA mutant would render the contorted conformation of the peptide backbone in the Gly462-Leu469 region of McrA considerably less stable (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from chemical properties and structural analysis.

claim: The thioamide sulfur is optimally distanced (3.6 Å) and geometrically positioned to form an H-bond with the side chain of Asn501 and the backbone N-H of Leu469.
source: The thioamide sulfur is also optimally distanced (3.6 Å) and geometrically positioned to form an H-bond with the side chain of Asn501 and the backbone N-H of Leu469.
evidence: This is observed from structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There appears to be a hydrophobic interaction between the thioamide and the beta carbon of Leu469.
source: There also appears to be a hydrophobic interaction between the thioamide and the beta carbon of Leu469, which would be energetically unfavorable with a more polarized amide.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: The thioglycine modification would be indispensable for thermophilic methanogens.
source: Based on this result, it seems reasonable to speculate that the thioglycine modification would be indispensable for thermophilic methanogens.
evidence: This is speculated based on the temperature-sensitive phenotype of the mutant.

claim: The ancestor of modern methanogens was likely a thermophilic organism.
source: It is often posited that the ancestor of modern methanogens was a thermophilic organism (Gribaldo and Brochier-Armanet, 2006; Forterre, 2015; Weiss et al., 2016; López-García et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from the literature with supporting citations.

claim: The universal presence of the thioglycine modification supports the thermophilic ancestry of methanogenesis.
source: Thus, the universal presence of the thioglycine modification supports the thermophilic ancestry of methanogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of the modification and evolutionary considerations.

claim: The ycaO-tfuA locus is conserved in Methanococcoides burtonii, a psychrophilic methanogen.
source: Indeed, the ycaO-tfuA locus is conserved even in Methanococcoides burtonii, a psychrophilic methanogen isolated from Ace Lake in Antarctica, where the ambient temperature is always below 2°C (Franzmann et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: MCR is essential for growth and survival of M. acetivorans.
source: As MCR is essential for growth and survival (Rother et al., 2005), the viability of ycaO-tfuA mutants precludes the hypothesis that the thioamide residue is essential for MCR activity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rother et al., 2005.

claim: The tryptic peptide at m/z 3432 Da contains a didehydroaspartate modification at Asp470.
source: This peptide also contains the recently reported didehydroaspartate modification at Asp470 (Wagner et al., 2016) and S-methylation at Cys472 (Selmer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The tryptic peptide at m/z 3432 Da contains S-methylation at Cys472.
source: This peptide also contains the recently reported didehydroaspartate modification at Asp470 (Wagner et al., 2016) and S-methylation at Cys472 (Selmer et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The archaeal TfuA proteins fall within a single clade that is largely congruent with the evolutionary history of archaea.
source: The archaeal TfuA proteins also fall within a single clade that is largely congruent with the evolutionary history of archaea (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2); however, unlike YcaO, the methanogen-containing clade includes numerous bacterial homologs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2.

claim: The methanogen-containing TfuA clade includes numerous bacterial homologs.
source: The archaeal TfuA proteins also fall within a single clade that is largely congruent with the evolutionary history of archaea (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2); however, unlike YcaO, the methanogen-containing clade includes numerous bacterial homologs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

source: Together, these processes produce and consume gigatons of methane each year, helping to establish the steady-state atmospheric levels of an important greenhouse gas.
